claim: The proboscis extension response (PER) consists of four major extension steps prior to food ingestion: lifting the rostrum, extending the haustellum, extending the labella, and spreading the labella.
source: Upon sucrose stimulation flies (1) lift the rostrum, (2) extend the haustellum, (3) extend the labella and (4) spread the labella to prepare for food intake (Figure 1A–F, Video 1 – see slow motion).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1A-F and Video 1, which document the sequential steps of proboscis extension in response to sucrose stimulation.

claim: The PER sequence is highly stereotypic both within individual flies and across multiple flies.
source: Importantly, this sequence was highly stereotypic both within individual flies and across multiple flies (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative temporal analysis shown in Figure 1G, which demonstrates consistent timing of movement steps across multiple flies and stimulations.

claim: Deviation from the stereotypic PER sequence occurred in only 4 out of 93 stimulations.
source: We observed a deviation from this sequence only in 4 out of 93 stimulations (n = 14 flies) in which labella extensions preceded haustellum extensions.
evidence: The claim is based on direct quantification of observed behavioral sequences across multiple experimental trials.

claim: The proboscis musculature consists of 17 individual muscles forming 13 major muscle groups.
source: Based on these data, the proboscis musculature consists of 17 individual muscles forming 13 major muscle groups.
evidence: This conclusion is based on anatomical analysis using muscle-specific GFP reporter (MHC-GFP) shown in Figure 2, which allowed visualization and counting of distinct muscle groups.

claim: Muscle group 2 is comprised of two independent muscles with unique attachment sites and different expression levels of the MHC-GFP reporter.
source: Analysis of the flanking muscles revealed that muscle 2 is comprised of two independent muscles with unique attachment sites and different expression levels of the MHC-GFP reporter (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation of muscle anatomy using fluorescent reporter expression shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The large muscle group 11 can be subdivided into three distinct muscle sets (11–1, 11–2, and 11–3) that attach to the upper sclerotized plate of the pharyngeal pump at unique angles.
source: In addition, our data shows that the large muscle group 11 can be subdivided into three distinct muscle sets (11–1, 11–2, and 11–3) that attach to the upper sclerotized plate of the pharyngeal pump at unique angles (Figure 2b').
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical visualization of muscle organization shown in Figure 2b'.

claim: Backfilling of proboscis nerves revealed 20 pairs of bilaterally symmetric motoneurons with somata arranged in two bilaterally symmetric clusters in the SEZ.
source: These experiments, recapturing an original analysis of Rajashekhar and Singh (1994), revealed 20 pairs of bilaterally symmetric MNs, with MN somata arranged in two bilaterally symmetric clusters in the SEZ (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by backfilling experiments shown in Figure 2D and references prior work by Rajashekhar and Singh (1994).

claim: All dendritic motoneuron arborizations are confined to the SEZ.
source: Consistent with prior reports we observe that all dendritic MN arborizations are confined to the SEZ.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations from backfilling experiments and is consistent with prior published reports.

claim: Proboscis motoneurons can only be recovered when heat-shock mediated flippase activation is induced during early embryogenesis (0–12 hr AEL) but not during late embryogenesis or larval stages.
source: Interestingly, we only recovered MN clones when heat-shock mediated flippase activation was induced during early embryogenesis (0–12 hr after egg-laying (AEL)) but not when the activation was performed during late embryogenesis or during larval stages.
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM experiments performed at different developmental time points.

claim: Multiple proboscis motoneurons were never recovered within a single brain hemisphere in MARCM analysis.
source: Furthermore, we never recovered multiple MNs within a brain hemisphere (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of 96 proboscis MN clones generated using MARCM technique.

claim: Eight motoneuron types innervate target muscles only on the ipsilateral side of the proboscis with respect to the soma.
source: Eight MN types innervate target muscles only on the ipsilateral side of the proboscis (with respect to the soma); these MNs innervate muscles that are involved in the extension, retraction, and positioning of the proboscis and mouthparts (this paper; Figures 2E and 3, and below).
evidence: The claim is based on single-cell MARCM analysis showing innervation patterns of individual motoneurons as documented in Figures 2E and 3.

claim: Four motoneuron types have axons that bifurcate and simultaneously innervate bilateral symmetric target muscles associated with the pharyngeal pump.
source: Strikingly, the axons of the remaining four MN types bifurcate and simultaneously innervate bilateral symmetric target muscles associated with the pharyngeal pump (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis showing bilateral innervation patterns documented in Figure 4.

claim: Muscle groups innervated by bifurcating motoneurons are thought to mainly control food ingestion and pumping.
source: These muscle groups are thought to mainly control food ingestion and pumping (Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published studies by Manzo et al., 2012 and Tissot et al., 1998.

claim: The proboscis is a serial homolog of other segmental appendages such as the thoracic legs.
source: The fly proboscis is an appendage of the head composed of highly reduced and bilaterally fused mouthparts that represents a serial homolog of other segmental appendages such as the thoracic legs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of insect morphology and developmental biology.

claim: The prothoracic leg is innervated by 53 motoneurons that derive from 11 independent neuroblasts.
source: The MNs innervating the prothoracic leg have been well characterized and comprise 53 MNs that derive from 11 independent neuroblasts, with two lineages giving rise to 35 of the 53 MNs (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published studies by Baek and Mann, 2009 and Brierley et al., 2012.

claim: Most leg motoneurons are generated postembryonically during larval development and match the development of the leg.
source: Most of these MNs are generated postembryonically during larval development and match the development of the leg (Estella and Mann, 2008; Estella et al., 2008; McKay et al., 2009; Morata, 2001; Soler et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple published studies on leg development.

claim: A hemi-proboscis is innervated by approximately 20 motoneurons.
source: In contrast, a hemi-proboscis is only innervated by approximately 20 MNs, and our MARCM labeling demonstrated that all MNs are born during embryogenesis (0–12 hr AEL).
evidence: The claim is based on backfilling experiments and MARCM analysis performed in this study.

claim: Each of the thirteen different proboscis motoneuron types are generated by different neuroblasts.
source: In contrast to the leg MNs, individual labeled clones never included more than one type of proboscis MN suggesting that each of the thirteen different MN types are generated by different neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from MARCM clonal analysis showing that single clones never contained multiple MN types.

claim: Gustatory stimulation elicits five consecutive, partially overlapping movements: rostrum lifting, haustellum extension, labella extension, labella spreading and proboscis retraction.
source: We show that gustatory stimulation elicits five consecutive, partially overlapping movements: rostrum lifting, haustellum extension, labella extension, labella spreading and proboscis retraction.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral analysis of proboscis extension in response to sucrose stimulation.

claim: Each step of proboscis extension is controlled by one bilateral pair of muscles that are innervated by one or multiple pairs of motoneurons.
source: Each of the steps is controlled by one bilateral pair of muscles that are innervated by one or multiple pairs of MNs.
evidence: The claim is based on combined anatomical and functional analysis of motoneurons and muscles.

claim: Artificial motoneuron activation was sufficient to elicit a single step of the serial proboscis motion in all cases.
source: In all cases, artificial MN activation was sufficient to elicit a single step of the serial proboscis motion.
evidence: The claim is based on optogenetic and thermogenetic activation experiments using TrpA1 and Chrimson.

claim: Initiation of individual proboscis movements does not depend on the execution of earlier steps of the motor sequence.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that initiation of individual movements does not depend on the execution of earlier steps of the motor sequence.
evidence: The claim is based on silencing experiments showing that subsequent steps can be executed despite blocking earlier steps.

claim: Serial execution of individual movements is necessary to achieve temporal precision of the PER sequence.
source: However, a serial execution of the individual movements is necessary to achieve temporal precision of the PER sequence as inihibition of individual MNs led to perturbations of the stereotypic temporal profile of the PER motion.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of PER sequences when individual motoneurons were silenced, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The movement of the proboscis elements is likely controlled in a one-to-one manner by individual motoneurons.
source: In contrast to a reflex chain as observed for crayfish escape behavior (Reichert et al., 1981) the movement of the proboscis elements is likely controlled in a one-to-one manner by individual MNs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from activation experiments and comparison to known reflex chain mechanisms in other organisms.

claim: The generation of the temporal proboscis motion sequence is programmed upstream of the motoneurons in the central brain.
source: Thus, our data indicates that the generation of the temporal proboscis motion sequence is programmed upstream of the MNs in the central brain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that individual motoneuron activation does not trigger subsequent movements.

claim: Different stereotypic proboscis movements are part of at least two additional innate behavior programs: male courtship behavior and proboscis cleaning.
source: This central coordination of MN activity is consistent with the observation that different stereotypic proboscis movements are part of at least two additional innate behavior programs. During male courtship behavior the proboscis displays an upward motion that includes rostrum lifting, labella extension and labella spreading (courtship licking) (Hall, 1994; Nichols et al., 2012) while the proboscis is placed outwards of the head capsule during proboscis cleaning (Hampel et al., 2015; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published observations of proboscis behavior in different behavioral contexts.

claim: GMR18B07 neurons are both sufficient and required for rostrum lifting.
source: Thus, the failure to lift the rostrum was indeed due to the acute inhibition of GMR18B07 neurons and not due to habituation or proboscis damage. In contrast to the efficient inhibition of rostrum lifting we did not observe a significant failure to spread the labella in these flies. Together, these results demonstrate that GMR18B07 neurons are both sufficient and required for rostrum lifting and at least partially involved in the control of labella spreading.
evidence: The claim is supported by both activation experiments (TrpA1 and Chrimson) and silencing experiments (shibirets) shown in Figure 5.

claim: GMR18B07 line expresses in one motoneuron pair innervating muscle 9 and another motoneuron pair innervating muscle 8.
source: Analysis of GMR18B07, repoGal80>mCD8-GFP flies revealed one MN pair innervating muscle 9, and another MN pair innervating muscle 8 (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical analysis using whole head preparation shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: MN2 controls the extension of the haustellum via activation of muscle 2–1.
source: Together these data indicate that MN2 controls the extension of the haustellum via activation of muscle 2–1.
evidence: The claim is based on combined activation and silencing experiments with GMR26A01 line, along with anatomical characterization showing innervation of muscle 2-1.

claim: MN6 controls extension of the labella via activation of muscle 6.
source: These results demonstrate that MN6 controls extension of the labella via activation of muscle 6.
evidence: The claim is based on activation and silencing experiments with GMR81B12 line shown in Figure 7.

claim: MN8 controls labella spreading.
source: Together, these results suggest that MN8 controls labella spreading but we cannot formally rule out the contribution of additional MNs.
evidence: The claim is based on activation experiments with multiple Gal4 lines (GMR18B07, GMR58H01, VT020958) that all express in MN8 and induce labella spreading.

claim: MN1 likely mediates active retraction of the proboscis into the head capsule.
source: Based on morphology and cross-comparison to the other MN lines we can exclude MN4, 7 and 8 indicating that MN1 likely mediates active retraction of the proboscis into the head capsule. Indeed, such a function has been previously suggested for MN1 in blowflies (van der Starre and Ruigrok, 1980).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from expression pattern analysis of GMR58H01 and comparison to prior literature on blowflies.

claim: Despite complete inhibition of rostrum lifting, flies were still able to extend the haustellum and labella.
source: For example, despite complete inhibition of rostrum lifting (MN9 silencing) flies were still able to extend the haustellum and labella (Figure 5B and Video 5).
evidence: The claim is based on silencing experiments shown in Figure 5B and Video 5.

claim: Blocking haustellum extension did not prevent extension or spreading of labella.
source: Similarly, blocking haustellum extension did not prevent extension or spreading of labella (Figure 6B and Video 8).
evidence: The claim is based on silencing experiments shown in Figure 6B and Video 8.

claim: Inhibition of rostrum lifting significantly prolonged the time from stimulus to haustellum extension but accelerated progression from labella extension to labella spreading.
source: Inhibition of rostrum lifting significantly prolonged the time from stimulus to haustellum extension but accelerated progression from labella extension to labella spreading (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of PER sequences shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of haustellum extension significantly reduced the time from rostrum lifting to labella extension and from labella extension to labella spreading.
source: Inhibition of haustellum extension significantly reduced the time from rostrum lifting to labella extension and from labella extension to labella spreading (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Full extension of the proboscis is not achieved by additive complete contractions of participating muscle groups but requires a precise temporal coordination of activation intensities.
source: These experiments demonstrate that full extension of the proboscis is not achieved by additive complete contractions of participating muscle groups but requires a precise temporal coordination of activation intensities.
evidence: The claim is based on experiments combining artificial motoneuron activation with sucrose-evoked proboscis extension shown in Figure 9.

claim: All proboscis motoneuron dendrites share a common space that mainly occupies the anteroventral regions of the SEZ with two spared 'ball like-structures' on both sides of the midline.
source: Analysis of the dendritic arborizations of these MNs revealed a stereotypic organization within the SEZ with all MN dendrites sharing a common space that mainly occupies the anteroventral regions of the SEZ with two spared 'ball like-structures' on both sides of the midline (Figure 10B–F, right panels; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical analysis of motoneuron dendritic patterns shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: MN9 is not directly connected to gustatory sensory neurons.
source: It has been previously reported that MN9 is not directly connected to gustatory sensory neurons (Gordon and Scott, 2009) that innervate posterior-dorsal regions of the SEZ (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Gordon and Scott, 2009.

claim: No significant GRASP signals were observed between proboscis motoneurons and Gr5a-expressing sweet gustatory sensory neurons.
source: To determine whether this observation holds true for all MNs we investigated potential connectivity of our MN lines to Gr5a-expressing sweet gustatory sensory neurons using the same GRASP approach (Feinberg et al., 2008). In these experiments, we did not observe significant GRASP signals (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on GRASP experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Control of the proboscis motor sequence is likely mediated via a dedicated set of interneurons downstream of gustatory sensory neurons.
source: Thus, control of the proboscis motor sequence is likely mediated via a dedicated set of interneurons downstream of gustatory sensory neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of direct connectivity between gustatory sensory neurons and motoneurons as shown by GRASP experiments.

claim: Activation of Gr5a sweet sensory neurons by expressing TrpA1 or Chrimson resulted in repetitive complete extensions of the proboscis mimicking natural activation by sucrose.
source: Artificial activation of Gr5a-Gal4 sweet sensory neurons by expressing either the heat-activatable Na+-channel TrpA1 (Hamada et al., 2008) or the red-shifted Channelrhodopsin2 Chrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) resulted in repetitive complete extensions of the proboscis mimicking natural activation by sucrose (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on artificial activation experiments shown in Video 2.

claim: Constant activation of MN9 caused a constant displacement of the proboscis consistent with the contraction of muscle 9.
source: In contrast, it has been reported that constant activation of MN9 caused a constant displacement of the proboscis consistent with the contraction of muscle 9 (Gordon and Scott, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Gordon and Scott, 2009.

claim: Unilateral activation of MN2 induced extension of the haustellum towards the activation side.
source: Furthermore, selective activation of an individual MN2 induced the extension of the haustellum towards the activation side (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on optogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sucrose stimulation of one leg induces proboscis extension towards the stimulus direction.
source: Indeed, similar to prior observations in the blowfly (Yetman and Pollack, 1987) sucrose stimulations of one leg induce proboscis extension towards the stimulus direction (Video 17).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations shown in Video 17 and comparison to prior literature on blowflies.

claim: Pharyngeal muscles on both sides are innervated by two bilateral homologous motoneurons with highly overlapping dendritic arborizations.
source: Thus, pharyngeal muscles on both sides are innervated by two bilateral homologous MNs with highly overlapping dendritic arborizations.
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM analysis showing that single MNs innervating muscle groups 11 and 12 bilaterally can have cell bodies in either brain hemisphere.

claim: The proboscis extension sequence during courtship licking lacks the haustellum extension step and consists only of rostrum lifting, labella extension and labella spreading.
source: For example, in contrast to the feeding motion the proboscis extension sequence during courtship licking lacks the haustellum extension step and consists only of rostrum lifting, labella extension and labella spreading.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of different behavioral contexts and inference about motor program differences.

claim: Flies display rhythmic patterns of proboscis extension and retraction when feeding on gelatinous food but not when drinking liquids.
source: Finally, analysis of natural feeding behavior demonstrated that flies display rhythmic patterns of proboscis extension and retraction when feeding on gelatinous food but not when drinking liquids. Thus, depending on the food quality a CPG contributes to the control of repetitive proboscis extension (Itskov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Itskov et al., 2014.

claim: At least 20 distinct motoneurons in each brain hemisphere control the activation of the 13 muscle groups contributing to either proboscis movement or pharynx-mediated food uptake.
source: Thus, at least 20 distinct MNs in each brain hemisphere control the activation of the 13 muscle groups contributing to either proboscis movement or pharynx-mediated food uptake.
evidence: The claim is based on backfilling experiments showing 20 pairs of motoneurons and anatomical analysis identifying 13 muscle groups.

claim: The entire dendritic arborization of MN6 is of dendritic nature within the SEZ.
source: Within the SEZ DenMark completely co-localized with mCD8-GFP indicating that the entire SEZ arborization is of dendritic nature (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on co-expression of the dendritic marker DenMark with membrane marker mCD8-GFP shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MN6 axons projecting through the labial nerve lack any DenMark expression.
source: The MN axons projecting through the labial nerve lacked any DenMark expression demonstrating the specificity of the marker.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of DenMark expression pattern shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Muscle 1 is innervated by multiple motoneurons.
source: Based on the co-staining with the postsynaptic muscle marker Discslarge (Dlg) it is evident that at least one additional MN innervates muscle 1.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemical analysis of neuromuscular junctions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MN9 has predominantly ipsilateral arborization with minor extensions to the contralateral side.
source: MNs 9 and 8 have predominantly ipsilateral arborization with minor extensions to the contralateral side (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM single-cell analysis shown in Figure 3C,F.

claim: MN7 has similar dendritic arborizations on both sides of the brain.
source: In contrast, MN7 has similar dendritic arborizations on both sides (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM single-cell analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MN6 displays predominant contralateral arborization with only minor extensions to the ipsilateral side.
source: while MN6 displays predominant contralateral arborization with only minor extensions to the ipsilateral side (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM single-cell analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All proboscis motoneurons strictly innervate ipsilateral located muscles but receive presynaptic input either predominantly ipsilateral, equal from both sides or predominantly from the contralateral side.
source: Thus, while all these MNs strictly innervate ipsilateral located muscles they receive presynaptic input either predominantly ipsilateral, equal from both sides or predominantly from the contralateral side.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of dendritic arborization patterns of different motoneuron types shown in Figure 3.

claim: The innervation pattern on the two homologous bilateral muscles by bifurcating motoneurons is almost identical.
source: These MNs display similar dendritic arborizations in both brain hemispheres and the innervation pattern on the two homologous bilateral muscles is almost identical (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: The claim is based on MARCM analysis of bifurcating motoneurons shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: Activation of a command interneuron is sufficient to induce the entire proboscis feeding motion.
source: This is supported by the observation that activation of an individual command interneuron is sufficient to induce the entire proboscis feeding motion (Flood et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Flood et al., 2013.

claim: The command neuron controlling proboscis feeding is not directly connected to motoneurons.
source: As this command neuron is not directly connected to MNs (Flood et al., 2013) the selective and sequential activation of the individual MNs requires at least an additional layer of interneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Flood et al., 2013.

claim: For peristaltic larval locomotion, the sequential and partially overlapping activation of intrasegmental motoneurons is controlled by both excitatory and inhibitory interneurons.
source: For peristaltic larval locomotion it has recently been demonstrated that the sequential and partially overlapping activation of intrasegmental MNs is controlled by both excitatory and inhibitory interneurons (Zwart et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Zwart et al., 2016.

claim: Motoneurons controlling distinct muscle groups in larval locomotion are innervated by largely non-overlapping excitatory interneurons.
source: The MNs controlling distinct muscle groups are innervated by largely non-overlapping excitatory interneurons similar to observations in vertebrates (Bikoff et al., 2016; Goetz et al., 2015; Tripodi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work on larval locomotion and vertebrate motor control.

claim: The phasic motoneuron activation delay in larval locomotion is mainly generated by selective inhibitory motoneuron innervation.
source: Interestingly, however, the phasic motoneuron activation delay is mainly generated by selective inhibitory MN innervation (Zwart et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Zwart et al., 2016.

claim: Flies display rhythmic patterns of proboscis extension and retraction when feeding on gelatinous food, indicating that a CPG contributes to the control of repetitive proboscis extension depending on food quality.
source: Finally, analysis of natural feeding behavior demonstrated that flies display rhythmic patterns of proboscis extension and retraction when feeding on gelatinous food but not when drinking liquids. Thus, depending on the food quality a CPG contributes to the control of repetitive proboscis extension (Itskov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on prior published work by Itskov et al., 2014.
